points.html: A unit (मात्रक) of measurement (मापन) is a definite magnitude of a quantity, defined and adopted by convention or by law.

In physics, power (शक्ति) is the rate of doing work (कार्य) or of transferring heat (ऊष्मा) or electrical energy (ऊर्जा) i.e. the amount of energy transferred or converted per unit (मात्रक) time. Power (P) = Time (t)Work (W) The SI unit of power is watt, which is equal to joule per second. Power is always represented in watt (W) or kilowatt (kW).

When a force (बल) acts to move an object, then work (कार्य) done by the force is equivalent to the product of force and displacement in the direction of force . It is a scalar quantity. The SI unit (मात्रक) of work is Newton metre, which is also called as joule. Joule is also the unit of Energy (ऊर्जा).

Unit (मात्रक) of radioactivity (रेडियोधर्मिता) is defined as the activity of a quantity of radioactive material where one decay takes place per second. The SI unit of radioactivity is becquerel (Bq) and this term is named after Henri Becquerel. Curie (Ci) is the old U.S. unit (non-S.I. unit) of radioactivity. Other pairs are correctly matched.
Light (प्रकाश)-year i s a unit (मात्रक) of astronomical distance equivalent to the distance that light travels in one year, which is 9.461 × 1015 metres.
It is used as a standard for measurement (मापन) of the same kind of quantity.

The parsec (symbol: pc) is a unit (मात्रक) of length used to measure the large distances to astronomical objects outside the Solar System, approximately equal to 3.262 light (प्रकाश)-years or ~ 206265 astronomical units (au), i.e. 30.9 trillion kilometres (19.2 trillion miles). A parsec is the distance from the Sun to an astronomical object that has a parallax angle...

Any other quantity of that kind can be expressed as a multiple of the unit (मात्रक) of measurement (मापन).

Acceleration (त्वरण) is the rate of change of velocity (वेग) of an object, with respect to time. The SI unit (मात्रक) of acceleration is metre per second square (m/s 2). The SI unit of force (बल) is newton (N). The SI unit of impulse is newton second (Ns). The SI unit of work (कार्य) is joule.

Light (प्रकाश) year is not a unit (मात्रक) of measuring time, but a unit of measuring distance. The remaining pairs are correctly matched.

points.html: Mechanics : Mechanics is that area of science concerned with the behaviour of physical bodies when subjected to force (बल) or displacements and the subsequent effects of the bodies on their environment.
Weight (भार) : Weight is the force (बल) exerted on a body by gravity (गुरुत्वाकर्षण)/ force with which the Earth attracts it.

Mass (द्रव्यमान) : Mass represents the amount of matter (measure of inertia) in a particle or an object. Mass remains the same everywhere (in Classical Mechanics). It is denoted by 'm'. Difference between Weight (भार) and Mass S.N. Weight (W) Mass (m) 1. 2. 3. 4. Gravitational (गुरुत्वाकर्षण) force (बल) of Earth It is a vector (वाहक) quantity. Weight varies according to places. Its SI unit (मात्रक) is newton (N). A measurement (मापन) of the amount of matter something contains It is a scalar quantity. It is constant at every place. Its SI unit is kilogram (kg). Distance & Displacement :
In daily language Distance & Displacement are used in the same sense but in Physics both have a different meaning.
The length of a specific path travelled between two points by an object is distance.
Displacement is the shortest distance measured from the initial to the final position of an object (along a straight line) and has direction from initial to final position.

Travelled distance has only magnitude, while displacement has magnitude along with the direction. It is clear that distance is a scalar quantity and displacement is a vector (वाहक) quantity. In a course of motion, the travelled distance by an object is not zero, but the final displacement may be zero. Displacement of an object will be zero when the moving object comes to its initial point. Speed (चाल) & Velocity (वेग) :

Speed (चाल) is the distance travelled per unit (मात्रक) of time. The average speed of an object is obtained by dividing the total distance by the total time taken. ∴ Average speed = Totalt imet akenTotalt ravelledd istance It is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is metre/second.

The reading of the balance increases if the person inhales deeply. One litre of air weighs about 1.225 g. A maximal 4.8 litre breath (average vital capacity for males) weighs approximately 5.88g. Inhaled air will add to the mass (द्रव्यमान) of the man and thus his weight (भार) goes up slightly.

The scalar quantity is defined as the quantity that has only got magnitude, but not directions whereas, vector (वाहक) quantity comprises of both magnitude and directions. Displacement, velocity (वेग) and force (बल) are the examples of vector quantity while volume is a scalar quantity.

Heat (ऊष्मा) always transfer from a substance of higher temperature (तापमान) to a substance of lower temperature. Measurement (मापन) of temperature :

points.html: In general physics, a free electron (इलेक्ट्रॉन) is an electron that can move under the influence of an applied electric (and/or magnetic) field rather than remaining bound to an atom (परमाणु) or molecule (अणु).
Metals with a high availability of free electrons/mobile charge carriers (and low scattering (प्रकीर्णन)) show high electrical conductivity (चालकता).
Silver has the highest electrical conductivity (चालकता) among common metals at room temperature (तापमान); copper, gold, and aluminium are also good conductors.
Electrical conduction (चालन) is also found in some liquids (e.g., electrolytes) and in gases when the gas becomes ionized (plasma (प्लाज्मा)/discharge).

In metals, conduction (चालन) is mainly due to the motion of electrons. In electrolytic liquids, conduction is mainly due to the motion of positive and negative ions. In ionized gases, conduction occurs due to electrons and ions.

Gases are generally poor conductors under ordinary conditions, but they conduct when sufficiently ionized. Gas breakdown/discharge depends on the electric field and on conditions such as the pressure (दाब)-gap product (Paschen-type behaviour); electrical discharges/arcs can occur even at atmospheric pressure (वायुमंडलीय दाब) (e.g., lightning, arc lamps/welding). Non-conductor :
Materials with very high electrical resistivity (very few free electrons/mobile charge carriers under normal conditions) are called insulators (non-conductors).
In insulators, electrons (and ions) are usually tightly bound and do not move easily, so current is extremely small under normal conditions.

points.html: Electric Conductivity (चालकता) :
Within the atom (परमाणु), electrons nearest to the nucleus are strongly bound to the positively charged nucleus (due to protons) by electrostatic attraction.
Electrons farther from the nucleus (outer/valence electrons) are comparatively less tightly bound.
Because they are less tightly bound, such outer electrons can be removed more easily (with sufficient external energy (ऊर्जा)).
In metals, some outer electrons become delocalized in the solid and act as ‘conduction (चालन) (free) electrons’.
Free (conduction (चालन)) electrons are electrons not bound to a particular atom (परमाणु) and are free to move through the material when an external electric field is applied.

In general physics, a free electron (इलेक्ट्रॉन) is an electron that can move under the influence of an applied electric (and/or magnetic) field rather than remaining bound to an atom (परमाणु) or molecule (अणु).
Metals with a high availability of free electrons/mobile charge carriers (and low scattering (प्रकीर्णन)) show high electrical conductivity (चालकता).

Electrical conductivity (चालकता) is a measure of the amount of electric current (विद्युत धारा) which a material can carry. The most electrically conductive element (तत्व) is silver followed by copper, aluminium and iron.

Copper rods are preferred for making lightning conductor because : (i) Copper is a better conductor of electricity than iron. (ii) Copper is not easily oxidized in the presence of oxygen and water molecules while iron gets rusted. (iii) Loss of energy (ऊर्जा) is much less with a copper rod than with iron rod, as copper is a bad conductor of heat (ऊष्मा) than iron.

A person travelling in a car with closed glass windows and doors is safe from the lightening strike, because closed car behaves like a closed hollow conductor (as a Faraday cage) and electric field or charge inside a closed conductor is always zero and hence, charges cannot enter inside the car.
Materials with very high electrical resistivity (very few free electrons/mobile charge carriers under normal conditions) are called insulators (non-conductors).
In insulators, electrons (and ions) are usually tightly bound and do not move easily, so current is extremely small under normal conditions.
Under sufficiently strong electric fields, an insulator (विद्युतरोधी) may conduct due to dielectric breakdown. Semiconductor (अर्धचालक) :
A semiconductor (अर्धचालक) is a material whose electrical conductivity (चालकता) lies between that of conductors and insulators.
Its conductivity (चालकता) can increase due to temperature (तापमान) (thermal generation of charge carriers) and due to controlled impurity addition (doping).
Adding controlled impurities to a semiconductor (अर्धचालक) is called doping; doped semiconductors are called extrinsic semiconductors.
Semiconductors typically show decreasing resistance (प्रतिरोध) with increasing temperature (तापमान), opposite to most metals.
Examples: Silicon, Germanium, Selenium, Tellurium (and α-Tin as a special elemental case). Superconductivity (अतिचालकता) :
If we could achieve superconductivity (अतिचालकता) at room temperature (तापमान) then we can save billions of rupee through electric transmission without any power (शक्ति) loss.

General Science  General Studies G–142 When superconductivity (अतिचालकता) was discovered in 1911, it was found only at temperatures close to absolute zero (– 273.15°C). Ceramic oxides play a vital role in the field of research and discovery towards superconductivity (अतिचालकता). Ceramic super conductive materials contain Mercury (Hg)/Thallium (Tl), Barium (Ba), Calcium (Ca) and Copper oxide (CO). Its discovery was first reported in 1993 and its transition temperature (तापमान) (Tc) was between 94 K-135 K.

With the increase in temperature (तापमान), the conductivity (चालकता) of the semiconductor (अर्धचालक) material increases. As with increase in temperature, outermost electrons acquire energy (ऊर्जा) and hence by acquiring energy, the outermost electrons leave the shell of the atom (परमाणु). Hence, with an increase in temperature, number of carriers in the semiconductor material increases which l...

High-pressure (दाब) hydrogen-rich materials have shown very high Tc values. In 2019 it was discovered that lanthanum decahydride (LaH10) shows superconductivity (अतिचालकता) at around 250-260 K under megabar pressures of around 168-180 gigapascals (GPa).

A 2020 claim of near room-temperature (तापमान) superconductivity (अतिचालकता) in “carbonaceous sulfur hydride” was later retracted (Nature, 26 Sep 2022), and a 2023 near-ambient claim in N-doped lutetium hydride was also retracted (Nature, 7 Nov 2023). Therefore, as of March, 2026, no room temperature superconductor is confirmed at ambient conditions, and the best-confirmed very-high T c results remain in high-pressure (दाब) hydrides such as LaH10. Nuclear fission (नाभिकीय विखंडन) is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei (fission fragments) of comparable masses, usually accompanied by neutrons and gamma radiation (विकिरण).
Sometimes neutrons are absorbed by a nucleus to form a heavier isotope; this is neutron (न्यूट्रॉन) capture, not nuclear fission (नाभिकीय विखंडन).
In fission, most energy (ऊर्जा) is released as kinetic energy (heat (ऊष्मा)) of the fission fragments; the remainder is carried by neutrons and gamma rays.

points.html: Launched in 2015, the mission aims to enhance India’s technological prowess in supercomputing, foster research and development (R&D), and support scientific advancements across academia, industry, and government sectors.

NSM was set up to provide the country with supercomputing infrastructure to meet the increasing computational demands of academia, researchers, MSMEs, and startups. It is a first of its kind attempt to boost the country’s computing power (शक्ति).

The Mission envisages empowering our national academic and R&D institutions spread over the country by installing supercomputers of various capacities. Access to these supercomputers is provided through the National Knowledge Network (NKN). The NKN is another program of the government which connects academic institutions and R&D labs over a high-speed (चाल) network.
Academic and R&D institutions as well as key user departments/ministries would participate by using these facilities and develop applications of national relevance.

The Mission also includes development of highly professional High-Performance Computing (HPC) aware human resource for meeting challenges of development of these applications. HRD activities in this area are steered through five training centres at Pune, Kharagpur, Chennai, Palakkad, and Goa to expand the awareness and G–163 General Studies  General Science familiarization of supercomputing with college students and researchers.

Under NSM, as of 30 November, 2025, a total of 37 supercomputers with cumulative compute capacity of 39 Petaflops, have been deployed across various academic institutions, research organizations, and R&D labs, including prominent institutions like IISc, IITs, C-DAC, and other institutions from Tier-II and Tier III cities of the country under NSM.

The supercomputing systems commissioned under NSM have achieved an overall utilization rate of over 85%, with many systems exceeding 95%, demonstrating a high level of usage and efficiency in their computational capacity.

NSM is steered jointly by Department of Science and Technology (DST) and Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and implemented by Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Pune and Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru. Classification of Computer :

The MTCR seeks to limit the risks of proliferation of weapons of mass (द्रव्यमान) destruction (WMD) by controlling exports of goods and technologies that could make a contribution to delivery systems (other than manned aircraft) for such weapons. In this context, the Regime places particular focus on rockets and unmanned aerial vehicles capable of delivering a payload of at least 500 kg to a range of at least 300 km and on equipment, software, and technology for such systems.

The MTCR is not a treaty and does not impose any legally binding obligations on Partners (members). Rather, it is an informal political understanding among states that seek to limit the proliferation of missiles and missile technology. The Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Pro- liferation (HCoC) :

The Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCoC) is the result of efforts of the international community to internationally regulate the area of ballistic missiles capable of carrying weapons of mass (द्रव्यमान) destruction (WMD).
The Hague Code of Conduct (HCoC), was established on 25 November, 2002 as an arrangement to prevent the proliferation of ballistic missiles.

The HCoC is the only multilateral code in the area of disarmament which has been adopted over the last years. The HCoC does not ban ballistic missiles, but calls for maximum possible restraint in the development, testing and deployment of ballistic missiles capable of delivering WMD.

Along with the MTCR, the HCoC is one of the only multilateral instruments addressing ballistic missile proliferation; the HCOC is the transparency and confidence building measure concerning the spread of ballistic missiles.

points.html: Albert Einstein (1879-1955) :

German-born physicist who developed the special and general theories of relativity and won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921 for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.
Einstein is generally considered the most influential physicist of the 20th Century. Einstein miracle year 1905 –
While working at the patent office, he did some of the most creative works of his life.

First Paper – He applied the quantum theory (Developed by German Physicist Max Planck) to light (प्रकाश) in order to explain the phenomenon known as the photoelectric effect, by which a material will emit electrically charged particles when hit by light.

Second Paper – Einstein's second paper of 1905, titled "On the Motion of Small Particles Suspended in a Stationary Liquid, as Required by the Molecular-Kinetic Theory of Heat (ऊष्मा)", provided a theoretical, mathematical explanation for Brownian motion. it provided crucial evidence for the existence of atoms and molecules, helping to convince skeptical physicists of their reality.

Third Paper – In the third and most famous article titled “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies” Einstein confronted the apparent contradiction between two principal theories of physics : Isaac Newton concepts of absolute space and time and James Clerk Maxwell’s idea (via electromagnetism) that the speed (चाल) of light (प्रकाश) is a constant. To do this he introduced his Special Theory of Relativity which held that the laws of physics are the same even for objects moving in different inertial frames (i.e. at constant speeds relative to each other) and that the speed of light is constant in all inertial frames.

Fourth paper concerned the fundamental relationship between mass (द्रव्यमान) and energy (ऊर्जा). Einstein famous equation E = mc2 (where ‘c’ is the constant speed (चाल) of light (प्रकाश)) expressed this relationship.

Bose, a graduate of the University of Calcutta taught at the University of Dhaka (1921-1945) and then at Calcutta (1945-1956). Bose’s numerous scientific papers published contributed to statistical mechanics and thermoluminescence and unified field theory. Bose’s Planck’s Law and the Hypothesis of Light (प्रकाश) Quanta (1924) led Einstein to seek him out for a collaboration.
A Fellow of the Royal Society, he was awarded India’s second-highest civilian award, the Padma Vibhushan, in 1954 by the Govt. of India.

ISCA has been promoting science and inculcating the spirit of science through its multifarious activities.

The ISCA vision is to inculcate scientific temper among the common people.

The ISCA mission is to make people aware about the recent developments in science and technology and its impact on the society, to establish different centres all over India for spreading scientific knowledge through school / college programs, to provide a common platform where scientists from India and abroad can exchange their views.

Masers are used as the timekeeping device in atomic clocks, and as extremely low-noise microwave amplifiers in radio telescopes and deep space spacecraft communication ground stations.

Modern masers can be designed to generate electromagnetic waves at not only microwave frequencies but also radio and infrared frequencies. For this reason Charles Townes suggested replacing "microwave" with the word "molecular" as the first word in the acronym maser.

A liquid crystal is a thermodynamically stable phase characterized by anisotropy of properties without the existence of a three-dimensional crystal lattice, generally lying in the temperature (तापमान) range between the solid and isotropic liquid phase, hence the term mesophase.

Liquid crystal materials are unique in their properties and uses. As research into this field continues and as new applications are developed, liquid crystals will play an important role in modern technology.

Liquid crystal materials generally have several common characteristics. Among these are a rod like molecular structure, rigidity of the long axis, and strong dipole and/ or easily polarizable substituents.
Liquid crystals find wide use in liquid crystal displays, which rely on the optical properties of certain liquid crystalline substances in the presence or absence of an electric field.

Liquid crystals have a multitude of other uses. They are used for nondestructive mechanical testing of materials under stress. This technique is also used for the visualization of RF (radio frequency (आवृत्ति)) waves in waveguides. They are used in medical applications where, for example, transient pressure (दाब) transmitted by a walking foot on the ground is measured. Low molar mass (द्रव्यमान) (LMM) liquid crystals have applications including erasable optical disks, full color "electronic slides" for computer-aided drawing (CAD), and light (प्रकाश) modulators for color electronic imaging. Neutron (न्यूट्रॉन) is a neutral particle which has no electrical charge. It was discovered by Chadwick in 1932. He discovered that when Beryllium (Be) or other atoms are bombarded with high speed (चाल) particles, then electrically neutral particles emerges from these atoms and such neutral particles are known as neutrons.

The particles that are smaller than the atoms are called sub- atomic particles. The three main sub-atomic particles that form an atom (परमाणु) are protons, neutrons and electrons. Deuteron contains a proton (प्रोटॉन) and a neutron (न्यूट्रॉन).
Atoms of different elements are with different atomic number.

The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom (परमाणु)’s nucleus is known as its mass (द्रव्यमान) number.
It is used as the nucleon count and approximates the atomic mass (द्रव्यमान) of a nuclide in atomic mass units.
Mass (द्रव्यमान) number of an atom (परमाणु) = No. of protons + No. of neutrons in nucleus of an atom.
It represents the total number of nucleons in the nucleus of an atom (परमाणु).
The mass (द्रव्यमान) number is not a fundamental character of the element (तत्व).

In particle physics, an elementary particle or fundamental particle is a subatomic particle with no sub-structure, thus not composed of other particles. Particles currently thought to be elementary include the fundamental fermions (quarks, leptons, antiquarks and antileptons) as well as fundamental bosons.

Neutrinos are one of the most abundant particles in the universe. Because they have very little interaction with matter, however, they are incredibly difficult to detect.

Different element (तत्व)’s atom (परमाणु) with the same number of neutrons are called Isoneutronic or Isotones. Radioactivity (रेडियोधर्मिता) is a nuclear phenomenon in which there is a spontaneous emission of radiations from the nuclei of atoms during their decay. In other words, radioactive decay is the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy (ऊर्जा) by radiation (विकिरण). Unstable nuclei that exist in nature are said to undergo natural radioactivity, and the man made unstable nuclei undergo artificial radioactivity.
The elements with such atoms have spontaneous disintegration character.
Such elements are called radioactive substances.
α particles, β particles and γ rays are emitted by radioactive nuclei. These three types of radiation (विकिरण) are called ionizing radiation.
Radioactivity (रेडियोधर्मिता) is a nuclear phenomenon, not a chemical reaction.
It was discovered by Henri Becquerel in Uranium.
In 1898 Marie Curie and her husband Pierre Curie discovered a radioactive element (तत्व) Polonium.

The Isotopes (समस्थानिक) are a set of nuclides/atoms having the same number of protons, but a different number of neutrons. In other words, the same atomic number (Z) but having different mass (द्रव्यमान) number (A). Each individual isotope has a separate nuclei. The Isotopes that are unstable and undergo radioactive decay are called radioisotopes.

points.html: Matter is defined as anything that occupies space and exhibits rest mass (द्रव्यमान) or inertia.

In physical changes no new substances are formed; the substance retains the same chemical composition while only its physical properties change. Physical changes may be reversible; some physical changes are irreversible, even though no new substance is formed.

In our daily life, we encounter many changes in our surroundings, though we do not notice them, such as souring of milk, rusting of iron, stretching of a rubber band, bread becoming toast, melting of wax, etc.
All these changes that take place around us are either a physical change or chemical change. Physical Changes
Physical changes, are the changes that change the physical traits of the substance, without making any change in their internal structure.

points.html: Several major attempts were made for classification of elements. Some of them are as follows - (i) Prout Hypothesis (1815-16) –
William Prout observed that the atomic weights that had been measured for the elements known at that time appeared to be whole multiples of the atomic weight (भार) of hydrogen.

He hypothesized that the hydrogen atom (परमाणु) was the only truly fundamental object, which he called protyle and that the atoms of other elements were actually groupings of various numbers of hydrogen atoms.

Later, more precise measurements of atomic weights showed many values were not exact integer multiples of hydrogen, so chemists rejected this simple form of the hypothesis, even though a modified ‘whole-number rule’ for isotopes (समस्थानिक) remains approximately valid. (ii) Dobereiner’s Law of Triads (1829) –

According to this law, when chemically analogous elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic weight (भार), they formed well-marked group of three called ‘Triads’, in which the atomic weight of middle element (तत्व) was nearly equal to the arithmetic mean of the other.

Periodic Table or Periodic table of elements is a tabular arrangement of the chemical elements, arranged by atomic number, electron (इलेक्ट्रॉन) configuration and recurring chemical properties, whose structure shows periodic trends. Need for classification of Elements :
Before the beginning of the 18 th century, only a few elements were known, so it was quite easy to study and remember the properties of those elements and their compounds individually.

Later on, with the growing number of known elements, it became more and more difficult to study their properties individually, therefore the need for their systematic classification was felt. Development of Periodic Table :
Several major attempts were made for classification of elements. Some of them are as follows - (i) Prout Hypothesis (1815-16) –
William Prout observed that the atomic weights that had been measured for the elements known at that time appeared to be whole multiples of the atomic weight (भार) of hydrogen.

He hypothesized that the hydrogen atom (परमाणु) was the only truly fundamental object, which he called protyle and that the atoms of other elements were actually groupings of various numbers of hydrogen atoms.

Later, more precise measurements of atomic weights showed many values were not exact integer multiples of hydrogen, so chemists rejected this simple form of the hypothesis, even though a modified ‘whole-number rule’ for isotopes (समस्थानिक) remains approximately valid. (ii) Dobereiner’s Law of Triads (1829) –

The most abundant element (तत्व) in the Universe is Hydrogen, which makes up about 3/4 of all matter. Helium makes up most of the remaining 1/4. Thus, it is clear that hydrogen is the most common and abundant element in the Universe. While the most abundant element in the Earth's crust is Oxygen making up 46.6% of Earth's crust.

All elements present in a group generally have similar electronic configuration in their valence shell and have the same number of valence electrons for main-group elements; transition metals are an important exception. Periods :
There are seven horizontal rows in the modern periodic table.
The elements in a period have consecutive atomic numbers.
The periods have been numbered from 1 to 7 (Arabic numerals).

In each period a new shell starts filling up. The period number is also the number of shells that starts filling up as we move from left to right across the period. (a) The first period is the shortest period of all. It contains only two elements – H and He. (b) The second and third periods are called short-periods each with 8 elements. (c) The 4th & 5th periods are called long periods each with 18 elements. (d) The 6th & 7th periods are very long periods; both presently have 32 known elements. Types of Elements :

points.html: The acid (अम्ल) name comes from Latin acidus which means sour and refers to the sharp odour and sour taste of many acids.
According to Arrhenius, acid (अम्ल) is a compound (यौगिक) that can increase the hydrogen-ion (H +/Hydronium-ion H 3O+) concentration in aqueous solution.

According to Bronsted - Lowry concept, acid (अम्ल) is defined as any hydrogen containing material which can donate a proton (प्रोटॉन) (hydron) to other substances. Properties of Acids : (i) Acids in solution have a pH below 7.0 (at about 25°C). (ii) Taste is sour. (iii) Releases hydrogen-ion (H+) in water. (iv) An acid turns blue litmus paper into red. (v) Chemicals or substances having the property of an acid are said to be acidic. Classification of acids :

Acids are divided into two main classes : I. Strong acids : These are completely ionized in water. They are very corrosive and can cause severe skin burns. Examples are hydrochloric acid (अम्ल) (HCl), Sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and nitric acid (HNO3). II. Weak acids : These are partially ionized in water. They are mildly corrosive and normally do not affect the skin. Examples are citric acid, acetic acid, tartaric acid etc. Sources of Some Natural Acids S.N. Name of Acid Source 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. Tartaric Acid Acetic acid (Ethanoic acid) Citric acid Oxalic acid Lactic acid Malic acid Ascorbic acid (Vitamin (विटामिन) C) Formic acid Grapes, Tamarind, Some citrus fruits, Bananas Vinegar Lemon, Orange and commonly in all citrus fruits Tomato, Spinach Curd Apple Amla, Guava, Papaya, Orange Stings of ants and Stinging Nettle (a plant) Uses of Acids : (i) Tartaric acid, lactic acid, acetic acid and malic acid are edible acids. (ii) Oxalic acid is used to remove the rust/iron stains on clothes. (iii) Conc.-Nitric acid is used in the preparation of explosive substances and for seperation of silver from gold-silver alloys. (iv) Aqua regia is a mixture (मिश्रण) of three-part of conc-hydrochloric acid and one part of conc-nitric acid (3 conc-HCl : 1 conc- HNO3). It has capacity to dissolve platinum and gold. It is also known as Royal water. It is primarily used to produce chloroauric acid for refining the highest quality of gold. It is also used in laboratories to remove trace amounts of organic compounds and trace metals from glassware. (v) Carbonic acid is (through carbonation of water from added CO2) present in soda and many soft drinks. (vi) Phosphoric acid is used as acidulant in Coca-Cola. (vii) Certain acids are used as drugs. Acetylsalicylic acid (Aspirin) is used as a pain-killer and for bringing down fever. Role of Acids in Human Body :

Acids play important roles in the human body. (i) The hydrochloric acid (अम्ल) present in the stomach (आमाशय) helps in the digestion (पाचन). (ii) Amino acids are the structural unit (मात्रक) of protein. For the synthesis of protein, amino acids are required. Protein is very essential for the growth and repair of body cells. (iii) Fatty acids are also required for growth and repair of body tissue. (iv) Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are essential for all known forms of life. Genes/DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) are responsible for transmitting of traits to offsprings from parents; RNA (ribonucleic acid) is involved in protein synthesis. (v) The carbonic acid/bicarbonate (H 2CO3/ HCO3
) buffer system is essential for the maintenance of pH equilibrium in the body. Base (क्षार) :
According to Arrhenius , a base (क्षार) is a compound (यौगिक) that increases the concentration of hydroxide ions (OH –) in aqueous solution.

According to Bronsted-Lowry concept, base (क्षार) is any substance that can accept a proton (प्रोटॉन) (hydron) from an acid (अम्ल)/ proton donor. Properties of Bases : (i) Bases have a bitter taste. (ii) Bases feel slippery. (iii) Bases conduct electricity in aqueous solution, because they consist of charged particles in solution. G–382 General Studies  General Science (iv) A water-soluble base is called an alkali if it produces OH– ions in water. (v) Bases in solution have a pH above 7.0 (at about 25°C). (vi) An alkali turns red litmus into blue. Some bases and their uses are as follows : (a) Calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)2–Slaked Lime (Limewater is saturated aqueous solution of this) (b) Ammonium hydroxide NH 4OH (Aqueous ammonia)–to clean glass windows. (c) Sodium hydroxide NaOH–used to prepare soap. (d) Potassium hydroxide KOH – used to prepare soap. (e) Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)2 – Its aqueous suspension is known as milk of magnesia, a common antacid. It is used to remove the acidity of the stomach (आमाशय) and also as a laxative. pH Scale :

points.html: In organic chemistry, a hydrocarbon (हाइड्रोकार्बन) is an organic compound (यौगिक) consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon.
Hydrocarbons from which one hydrogen atom (परमाणु) has been removed are univalent substituent groups called hydrocarbyls, e.g. Methyl, phenyl etc.
In hydrocarbons the carbon atoms join together to form the framework of the compound (यौगिक) and the hydrogen atoms attach to them in many different configurations.
Hydrocarbons are the principal constituents of petroleum and natural gas.
Hydrocarbons serve as fuels and lubricants as well as raw materials for the production of plastics, fibres, rubbers, solvents, explosives and industrial chemicals.

Many hydrocarbons occur in nature. In addition to making up fossil fuels, they are present in trees and plants. For example in the form of pigments called carotene (C40Hx e.g. β-carotene C40H56) that occur in carrots and green leaves.

points.html: The hydrocarbons, which contain carbon atoms linked on the non-cyclic (acyclic) open-chain are known as open- chain hydrocarbons. In these hydrocarbons, the chain of carbon atoms is not cyclic.
Open-chain hydrocarbons are further divided into (i) Saturated hydrocarbons (ii) Unsaturated hydrocarbons (i) Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes):
Those hydrocarbons, in which the carbon atoms are bonded to each other with a single covalent bond (–C–C–) are called a cyclic saturated hydrocarbons. They are also known as alkanes.
They follow the general formula CnH2n+2 (–ane suffix). For example-methane, ethane, propane, etc.
They are also known as paraffin because these are less reactive in normal conditions with acids and other reagents (Parum = too little, Affinis = related → little affinity). Methane (CH4) :
Methane is the first member of open chain saturated hydrocarbons.

Methane is the primary constituent of natural gas and it is released into the atmosphere from crude oil production and some industrial activities. More of it is released from biological processes. It is also known as Marsh gas due to its production in the wetland by decomposition of organic materials by anaerobic archaea (methanogens). points.html: Alcohol is an organic compound (यौगिक) with a hydroxyl (–OH) functional group attached to a saturated carbon atom (परमाणु). Because –OH is the functional group of all alcohols, we often represent alcohols by the general formula R-OH where R is an alkyl group.
In other words, the hydroxyl derivatives of alkenes/ aliphatic hydrocarbons are termed as alcohols.

Condensed/structural formula and name of some alcohols are as follows : (i) Methyl Alcohol (Methanol) – CH3OH (ii) Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol) – C2H5OH (iii) n-Propyl Alcohol – CH3CH2CH2OH (iv) Isopropyl Alcohol – (CH3)2CHOH (v) n-Butyl Alcohol – CH3 (CH2)2CH2OH (vi) Isobutyl Alcohol – (CH3)2CHCH2OH Methyl Alcohol (Methanol or Carbinol) :
Its chemical formula is CH3OH.
It acquired the name wood alcohol or wood naphtha because it was once produced primarily by the destructive distillation of wood.
Today it is mainly produced by hydrogenation of carbon monoxide.
It is the simplest alcohol, consisting of a methyl group linked to a hydroxyl group.
It is light (प्रकाश), volatile, colourless, flammable liquid with a distinctive odour similar to that of ethanol (Ethyl alcohol).
Methyl alcohol (CH 3OH) is also called wood spirit. It is obtained by the destructive distillation of wood.

It is used in the preparation of the methylated spirit. A mixture (मिश्रण) of methyl alcohol and ethyl alcohol is known as methylated spirit or denatured alcohol, which is not suitable for drinking.

The mixture (मिश्रण) of methyl alcohol (40%) and water (60%) is used earlier in radiators of automobiles as antifreeze . Modern automobile engine coolants are predominantly ethylene-glycol based. Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol) :

Barley, water, hops and yeast are the four magic ingredients that are required for making beer. Other grains like maize, rice, rye and wheat are also used in making beer. Whisky is also made from fermented barley grains.

The word ‘Science’ comes from the Latin word ‘scientia’, meaning ‘knowledge’.
Science is the systematic knowledge of the physical or material world gained through observation and experimentation.
Science has been classified into– (1) Natural Sciences and (2) Social Sciences.
The natural sciences comprise the physical sciences, Earth and space sciences, and life (biological) sciences; life sciences (biology) are further divided into many branches and sub-branches.

Lamarck and Treviranus introduced the term ‘biology’ independently in modern sense in 1802. Branches and Subbranches of Biology Zoology – Detailed study of the members of the animal kingdom and animal life in general. Botany – Detailed study of plants and their life. Palaeontology – The study of history of life on Earth as based on fossils. Fossils are preserved remains, impressions, or traces of plants, animals, and other organisms from the geologic past; they may be preserved in Earth’s crust and also by processes such as drying, freezing, and entrapment in amber or asphalt. Palaeobotany – Study of plant fossils. Ecology – The branch of biology that deals with the relation of organisms to one another and to their physical surroundings. Genetics – The study of heredity (आनुवंशिकता) or how the characteristics of living things are transmitted from one generation to the next. In living organisms, DNA is the genetic material. This material is passed on when organism reproduces. The basic unit (मात्रक) of heredity is ‘Gene (जीन)’. Physiology – Study of normal functions of living creatures and their parts. Pedology – It is the study of soils in their natural environment. It deals with pedogenesis, soil morphology and soil classification. Edaphology – It concerns with the influence of soils on living things, particularly plants. Gerontology – Study of the social, cultural, physiological, cognitive, and biological aspects of ageing, or the scientific study of old age, the process of ageing and the particular problems of old people. Ethology – It is the scientific and objective study of non-human animal behaviour usually with a focus on behaviour under natural conditions, and viewing behaviour as an evolutionary adaptive trait. Bionics – It is the study of mechanical systems that function like living organisms or parts of living organisms. Bionics is the application of biological methods and systems found in nature to the study and design of engineering systems and modern technology. The word ‘bionic’ was coined by Jack E. Steele in 1958. Bionomics – The study of the mode of life of organisms in their natural habitat and their adaptations to their surroundings. Bionomics is the comprehensive study of an organism and its relation to its environment. It is also referred as ‘ecology’. Bionomy – Branch of biology concerned with the laws of life. Biometry – It is also known as biostatistics. It is the development and application of statistical and mathematical methods to analyse the data results from biological observations and phenomenon. Phrenology – The detailed study of the shape and size of the cranium as a supposed indication of character and mental abilities. Anthology – Study of flowers. It is also used for a collection of selected writings/works. Agrostology – It deals with the scientific study of true grasses. It is also called Graminology – scientific study of grasses (the family Poaceae or Gramineae). Palynology – The study of pollen grains and other spores especially as found in archaeological or geological deposits. Pollen extracted from such deposits may be used for radiocarbon dating and for studying past climates and environments by identifying plants then growing. Oncology – A branch of biology (Medicine) that deals with the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of tumours/cancer. Teratology – The scientific study of congenital abnormalities and abnormal formations.
